lead: The echo from a target is unimaginably weak. A radar may send hundreds of kilowatts, yet the power that returns is often picowatts. The radar range equation explains why. It follows power from the transmitter, through the spreading beam, off the target, back through space and into the antenna. The result links transmit power, antenna gain, wavelength, target cross section and receiver sensitivity to one useful number: the greatest range at which the target can be detected. Air-traffic control, weather radar and missile tracking all use this budget.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the radar block diagram, and Unit 2 for gain, effective aperture and the Friis spreading-loss idea.

blocks.text: Take a monostatic radar: one antenna transmits and receives. The transmitter delivers P<sub>t</sub> watts to an antenna of gain G. G is a ratio, not dB. On the beam axis at range R metres, the power density is S = P<sub>t</sub>G/(4πR²), in W/m². The 4πR² is the area of a sphere of radius R; the gain multiplies the density in the beam direction.

The target intercepts power equal to S times its radar cross section σ, in square metres. Think of σ as an equivalent capture area, not the physical size; Chapter 6.3 explains it. If the target scatters this power equally in all directions, the density back at the radar is PtGσ/((4π)²R⁴). Two spreads by R² give the R⁴.

The receiving antenna does not collect all that density. It has an effective aperture A<sub>e</sub> in m², so the received power is P<sub>r</sub> = S<sub>return</sub>A<sub>e</sub>. Use the antenna relation G = 4πA<sub>e</sub>/λ², with λ the wavelength in metres. Substitute A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/(4π):

blocks.where: P<sub>r</sub> is received echo power in W; P<sub>t</sub> is transmitted power in W; G is antenna gain as a ratio; λ is wavelength in m; σ is radar cross section in m²; R is target range in m.

blocks.text: The same result in terms of aperture is P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>A<sub>e</sub>²σ/(4πλ²R⁴). This form is handy when the antenna is described by its physical area. Notice G appears squared: one G for the transmit beam, one G for the receive capture. That square is the most common slip in exams.

sections.h3: The weakest echo the receiver can see

blocks.text: Set P<sub>r</sub> equal to the minimum detectable signal S<sub>min</sub>. The receiver cannot declare a target from an echo weaker than its own noise. For a receiver with noise figure F as a ratio, noise bandwidth B in Hz, and reference temperature T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K, the noise power is

blocks.where: k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant; T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K; F is noise figure as a ratio; B is noise bandwidth in Hz; S<sub>min</sub> is in W.

blocks.text: Losses reduce the echo before it reaches the detector. Cable loss, duplexer loss, radome loss and signal-processing loss are collected into a system loss factor L, a ratio greater than 1. Put L in the denominator: the effective received power is P<sub>r</sub>/L.

A single pulse may be too weak, so the radar integrates n pulses. Coherent integration adds the echoes with the right phase; the signal-to-noise power ratio rises as n. Noncoherent integration, such as a square-law detector, gives less: roughly √n at low signal-to-noise ratio and closer to n at high signal-to-noise ratio, depending on the detector. Use n as the optimistic case and √n as the cautious case.

sections.h3: Maximum range and the fourth-power law

blocks.text: Set P<sub>r</sub>/L = S<sub>min</sub> and solve for R. The result is the radar range equation in its maximum-range form:

blocks.where: R<sub>max</sub> is maximum detectable range in m; the other symbols are as above; L is the system loss ratio.

blocks.text: With effective aperture directly, R<sub>max</sub> = [P<sub>t</sub>A<sub>e</sub>²σ/(4πλ²S<sub>min</sub>L)]<sup>1/4</sup>. Use whichever antenna description you have. Do not mix the two forms: the (4π)³ form needs G, the other needs A<sub>e</sub>.

The fourth root governs performance. Double the range and R⁴ rises by 2⁴ = 16, so the transmitter needs 16 times the power, or 12 dB more. Increase σ one hundredfold and R<sub>max</sub> rises by 100<sup>1/4</sup> = 3.16, not 100. Plotted against range, the echo power falls as 1/R⁴; plotted against σ, range rises as σ<sup>1/4</sup>, as the figure shows.

A search radar must cover a volume, not one target. Its equation replaces single-pulse power by average power and adds search solid angle and search time. Only a few universities teach this form; the three-line idea is that the search equation answers 'how far can I search a volume per second', while the range equation answers 'how far can I detect one target'.

figure.caption: Maximum range against target cross section for the worked example. A hundredfold rise in σ from 1 m² to 100 m² moves maximum range only from about 38.8 km to about 122.7 km.

spec.aria: Curve of maximum radar range against target cross section, showing that a hundredfold rise in cross section only triples the range because range depends on the fourth root.

examples.question: A monostatic radar transmits P<sub>t</sub> = 500 kW at 10 GHz. The antenna gain is 30 dB. It must detect a target with radar cross section σ = 1 m². The minimum detectable signal is S<sub>min</sub> = 1 × 10⁻¹³ W and system loss is 0 dB. (a) Find the wavelength. (b) Find R<sub>max</sub>. (c) Find the transmitter power needed to double this range.
steps: 7. Doubling range multiplies R⁴ by 16, so P<sub>t</sub> must be 16 × 500 kW = 8 MW.
examples.answer: R<sub>max</sub> is about 38.8 km, and doubling it needs 8 MW of transmitter power.
examples.check:
import math
Pt = 500e3
f = 10e9
G_db = 30
sigma = 1.0
Smin = 1e-13
L = 1.0
c = 3e8
lam = c/f
G = 10**(G_db/10)
num = Pt*G**2*lam**2*sigma
den = (4*math.pi)**3*Smin*L
R4 = num/den
R = R4**0.25
print(f"{lam:.2f}")
print(f"{G:.0f}")
print(f"{num:.3e}")
print(f"{den:.3e}")
print(f"{R4:.3e}")
print(f"{R:.0f}")
print(f"{R/1000:.1f}")
print(f"{16*Pt/1e6:.1f}")

traps: Using received power P<sub>r</sub> in place of S<sub>min</sub> when solving for R<sub>max</sub>. The equation gives maximum range only when P<sub>r</sub> equals the weakest detectable echo.
Forgetting that G is squared. In the monostatic form one G is the transmit beam and one is the receive capture; a 3 dB gain error becomes 6 dB in the echo.
Doubling range needs 16 times the power, not 2 times. In dB that is 12 dB more transmit power.
Putting F in dB into S<sub>min</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>FB. F must be a ratio; 10 dB means F = 10.
Mixing kilometres and metres, or using λ in cm. R and λ must be in the same length unit, preferably metres.

quiz.q: State the radar range equation for a monostatic radar and define each symbol.
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G²λ²σ/((4π)³R⁴); P<sub>t</sub> transmit power in W, G gain ratio, λ wavelength in m, σ cross section in m², R range in m, P<sub>r</sub> received power in W.

quiz.q: Why does a hundredfold increase in σ raise R<sub>max</sub> only by about 3.16?
quiz.a: R<sub>max</sub> is proportional to σ<sup>1/4</sup>. The fourth root of 100 is 100<sup>1/4</sup> = 3.16.

quiz.q: A radar has R<sub>max</sub> = 20 km. By what factor must P<sub>t</sub> increase to reach 40 km?
quiz.a: Range doubles, so R⁴ rises by 2⁴ = 16. P<sub>t</sub> must increase 16 times.

quiz.q: Keeping P<sub>t</sub>, G, σ and S<sub>min</sub> fixed, the frequency is raised from 3 GHz to 12 GHz. Find the new R<sub>max</sub> as a fraction of the old.
quiz.a: Frequency rises 4 times, so λ falls to 1/4. R<sub>max</sub> is proportional to λ<sup>1/2</sup>, so the new range is (1/4)<sup>1/2</sup> = 1/2 of the old range.

quiz.q: A receiver has F = 10 dB, B = 1 MHz, T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K. Find S<sub>min</sub>.
quiz.a: F = 10 as a ratio. S<sub>min</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>FB = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 10 × 10⁶ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ W.

quiz.q: Compare coherent and noncoherent integration of n pulses.
quiz.a: Coherent integration gives a signal-to-noise power ratio rise of n. Noncoherent integration gives between about √n and n, depending on the detector and the signal-to-noise ratio.

quiz.q: A target at 40 km returns echo power P<sub>r</sub>. If its RCS falls to 1/16 of the old value, at what range does the same P<sub>r</sub> occur?
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub> is proportional to σ/R⁴, so R⁴ is proportional to σ. R falls by (1/16)<sup>1/4</sup> = 1/2, giving 20 km.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern radars trade one high-power tube for many solid-state modules and digital beamforming, but the same fourth-root budget decides the design. Search terms: radar range equation, fourth-root law, search radar equation, noise figure, coherent integration. Newer curricula add clutter and detection probability, which come later in this unit.
